en: The Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva said to Ānanda: "In my teaching, there is one who contemplates with sovereign ease (Avalokiteśvara).

Through transformation, he reaches contemplation from within the mind and attains self-mastery. His contemplative hearing is perfectly luminous; his wisdom is unimpeded. He contemplates existence without dwelling in existence. He contemplates...
Emptiness does not abide in emptiness. The mind cannot be moved; objects cannot follow it. Though there is movement and following, its truth remains undisturbed;
thus one attains great sovereign mastery and perfect penetration. "Bodhisattva" is an abbreviation of *bodhisattva*.
*Bodhi* means awakening; *sattva* means sentient being. It refers to one who can awaken all sentient beings—awakening oneself and awakening others.
"Bodhisattva" and "Mahāsattva" are both honorific titles for the name of the Buddha.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva is none other than the Mahāsattva Guanyin.
"When practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*": "practicing the profound" means that the practice of the dharmas of the pure causal ground has already deepened.

When one's meritorious practice is most profound and one possesses great wisdom, reaching the further shore (*pāra*), "much" refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and "time" refers to the opportune moment.
At this time, the Bodhisattva’s wondrous enlightenment is perfectly luminous, transcending the world, and fully endowed with [all virtues].
This is the time when one attains the samādhi of wisdom through the feet of practice.

One clearly perceives that the five aggregates are all empty. "Clearly perceiving" (*zhào*) refers to the wisdom of the fundamental mind, the wondrous awakening and luminous illumination. "Perceiving" (*jiàn*) refers to—

The wisdom of the original mind is the luminous, perfect, and true vision. The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) refer to the five *skandhas* of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Emptiness is the essential substance of the original mind; it is the true emptiness of the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*).
When one perceives that the aggregates are empty, the wondrous luminosity of the original mind is revealed, and the essential substance of its nature is clearly seen.
"To cross over all suffering and calamity" means to liberate oneself from all attachments— the suffering and calamities of birth, death, and affliction—
and to achieve complete and perfect penetration in all things.
Śāriputra—whose mother’s name was Śārī, and who was thus named after her—is a disciple of the Buddha who is foremost among the Buddha’s disciples in wisdom.
Yet, he was unable to attain ultimate realization of perfect penetration and achieve right enlightenment like Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; this was because he remained stuck in...
It is wisdom. Yet, if one becomes stagnant in wisdom, there will be the marks of self and views of self, as well as the marks of emptiness and views of emptiness.

Therefore, the Buddha [taught] the practice of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara regarding the profound *prajñāpāramitā*—the dharma of true emptiness and signlessness—in order to realize the other shore of Bodhi and to attain the standard of universal illumination and perfect clarity. He then addressed Śāriputra, saying:
It is desired that they do not become obstructed by the mark of self (*ātman*) or the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), nor by the mark of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) or the view of emptiness (*śūnyatādṛṣṭi*),
but rather ultimately reach the realm of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), thereby realizing the unsurpassed path.
Form is not different from emptiness; form is like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a shadow, and therefore it is not different from emptiness.
Emptiness is not different from form; emptiness is the manifestation of the single truth, and therefore it is not different from form.
Form is itself emptiness. Form possesses characteristics; whatever has characteristics is entirely illusory and will ultimately reach a time of destruction.
Therefore, form is itself emptiness.
Emptiness is precisely form. Emptiness is void and non-existent, without shape and without sound. The Way takes this void and non-existent substance as its essence;
it cannot be seen when looked upon, nor heard when listened to, yet it is able to give rise to the ten thousand things of heaven and earth, which possess both form and sound.
Therefore, emptiness is precisely form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so. Because of form, there arises the reception by the six sense organs.
The six sense organs receive this within the mind, giving rise to the perception (*saṃjñā*) that deliberates and speculates, which hangs upon the characteristics of the six objects.

From this, there arise the mental formations (*saṃskāra*) that engage in activity and application. Through these movements and transitions, there arises the consciousness (*vijñāna*) that discriminates between the refined and the coarse, the beautiful and the ugly.

The five aggregates—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—are mutually dependent. When form undergoes destruction, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise ultimately revert to emptiness and falsehood;
thus, form is itself emptiness. If one can fully realize that form is emptiness, then upon encountering form, one will not grasp it.
Consequently, there will be no various discursive thoughts of sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; the single mind will be pure and empty.
If the great void gives rise to the true mark of ultimate emptiness through the absence of marks, it is likewise so:
emptiness is itself form.
Śāriputra—[the Buddha] calls out the name of Śāriputra and advances one further step.
This is what he informs them. His intention is that not only are the five aggregates empty, but all dharmas for the cultivation and realization of bodhi are likewise empty.
Being neither born nor extinguished, the true nature remains indestructible throughout kalpas; therefore, it is neither born nor extinguished.
Neither defiled nor pure. The true nature is originally unstained; therefore, it is neither defiled nor pure.
Neither increasing nor decreasing. The true nature does not cling to a single thing; being naturally sufficient as it is, it neither increases nor decreases.
"Therefore, in emptiness there is no form. This is a phrase that takes up what precedes it to initiate what follows.
Therefore, within true emptiness, there is fundamentally no mark of self; how could there be any form?
There is no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Since there is no mark of self, one naturally lacks the view of self.
How could all sounds and forms enter my heart of wondrous clarity and true emptiness? For oneself, there is already no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. Since the mark of self does not exist, the six sense faculties are likewise not mine;
thus, there is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
There is no form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental object. Since the six sense faculties do not exist, the six sense objects do not exist either—this is the place of rest.
From the absence of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects;

there is no eye-element (*cakṣur-dhātu*), and so on, up to the absence of the consciousness-element (*vijñāna-dhātu*). Furthermore, that which is perceived by the eyes is designated as the eye-element, and that which the mind directs toward is designated as the consciousness-element.
The eye is the vanguard of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), and the mind is the [vanguard] of the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*).

The Lord General. Thus, when the six faculties and six objects have no consciousness that does not manifest, and there is no realm of the eye up to no realm of mental consciousness, then the eighteen realms—the six faculties, six objects, and six consciousnesses—are all devoid of boundaries.

Now that the realm of the eye is empty, all conditions are utterly extinguished and mental consciousness is completely forgotten; one will then see [the state] proceeding from meditative concentration to stillness.
Tranquil yet wise, there is neither ignorance nor the exhaustion of ignorance; there is no ignorance, and there is no exhaustion of ignorance.
That which is "without" refers to the absence of deluded and obscure thoughts.
...up to and including no aging and death. Through long duration it becomes firm; through firmness it becomes constant. "No aging and death" means eternally existing and indestructible.

Furthermore, there is no exhaustion of aging and death. From ignorance to aging and death—this is what the Buddha taught as the twelve links of dependent origination throughout the three periods of time.
These are the conditions (*pratyaya*). First is ignorance (*avidyā*), which refers to the past life; it is the delusion of false consciousness regarding its true nature.

Second is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), which refers to all karmic fetters and activities in the past life that flow and revolve following the false consciousness of ignorance. Third is consciousness (*vijñāna*), which refers to the present life;
it is the spiritual seed of the consciousness that takes rebirth in the womb. Fourth is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), which refers to the present life; it is [the development of] consciousness...
The spirit resides within the womb; the mind exists as a mere name, yet the physical body already possesses substance. Fifth is the "six entrances" (*ṣaḍāyatana*): this refers to the present life.
While the spirit and consciousness reside in the womb, the substance of the six sense organs has already been formed, and the functions of the six entrances have already been established.
Sixth is "contact" (*sparśa*): this refers to the present life after the physical body has emerged from the womb; the six sense organs merely possess [their respective objects].
*Sparsa* (Contact): One has not yet fully understood the engagement with the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Seventh is *vedanā* (Feeling):
This refers to the present life, when the physical body gradually grows larger and is already able to receive the various objects of the six sense fields;

however, the mind has not yet given rise to craving, lust, and so forth. Eighth is *tṛṣṇā* (Craving): This refers to the present life, when the physical body becomes increasingly mature, and [cravings such as] lust and so forth [arise].
The mind has already opened and various forms of craving arise; however, the realm of craving has not yet been fulfilled. Ninth is *upādāna* (clinging):

this refers to the present life, when the physical body is robust and craving grows ever more intense, such that one rushes about and indulges in seizing forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles, thereby fulfilling the realm of craving.
Tenth is *bhava* (existence): this refers to the present... form.

The body, through the unrestrained pursuit of sensory objects, accumulates the causes for the three realms—the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Thus, the karmic fruits of the three existences—desire-existence, form-existence, and formless-existence—are brought to fulfillment. Eleventh is birth:
this refers to the fact that cause and effect do not perish; consciousness and spirit follow the flow of karma to undergo birth, aging, and decay. Furthermore...
One dies after being broken [by decay]. Conditioned by ignorance, there are volitional formations; conditioned by volitional formations, there is consciousness;

conditioned by consciousness, there is name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form, there are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases, there is contact; conditioned by contact, there is feeling; conditioned by feeling, there is craving; conditioned by craving, there is clinging;
conditioned by clinging, there is becoming; conditioned by becoming, there is birth; conditioned by birth, there are old age and death. These are the twelve links of dependent origination.

Dependent origination is characterized by arising and ceasing, impermanence, having a beginning and an end; it ends and then arises again, it arises and then ends again, revolving through the three periods of time in a cycle of birth and death.

If one contemplates these twelve links of dependent origination and clearly realizes that they are all the deluded consciousnesses of the unconditioned flowing forth, and suddenly awakens to the fact that the eighteen realms are all empty, then the fundamentally wondrous and luminous mind will be as it truly is, in its state of suchness.

Movement. When there is no deluded consciousness of arising and ceasing, then there is no "non-existence of ignorance" (avidyā-akṣaya). Since there is no non-existence of ignorance, there is neither arising nor exhaustion;
thus, there is also no exhaustion of ignorance. "And so forth" means: there is no formation of form (*rūpa*), nor is there an exhaustion of formation;

there is no consciousness (*vijñāna*), nor is there an exhaustion of consciousness; there is no name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), nor is there an exhaustion of name-and-form; there is no six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), nor...

There is no exhaustion of the six sense bases; there is no contact, nor is there an exhaustion of contact. There is no feeling, nor is there an exhaustion of feeling. There is no craving, nor is there an exhaustion of craving.
There is no grasping, nor is there an exhaustion of grasping. There is no existence, nor is there an exhaustion of existence.
There is no birth, nor is there an exhaustion of birth. There is no aging and death, nor is there an exhaustion of aging and death.

There is no suffering (duḥkha) or its accumulation (samudaya). "Suffering" refers to the various sufferings of birth-and-death and afflictions (kleśa). "Accumulation" refers to the gathering together.

When a person lives in this world, the mind is enslaved by the body, and the body is exhausted by worldly affairs. One accumulates the bases (āyatana), objects (viṣaya), and elements (dhātu) within the five aggregates (pañcaskandha), as well as the twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda)—the various causes of birth-and-death, afflictions, and suffering.
Now that the five aggregates, bases, objects, and elements are absent, [there is no suffering].
Regarding the realms and the twelve links of dependent origination, there is no accumulation of the causes of suffering.
As for cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*): "cessation" refers to the extinction of the origin of suffering; "the path" refers to the true, eternal, and unceasing Way.

Within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), all causes of suffering are individually subject to arising and ceasing, and are impermanent. Now that this arising and ceasing has been extinguished, quiescent cessation (*śānta-nirodha*) manifests before one. And...

The wondrous luminosity of its very substance is the true nature of quiescence; it is penetratingly pervasive and perfectly unobstructed, whereby one enters the Great Way of eternal constancy and ceaseless activity.
There is neither wisdom nor attainment; that is to say, since there is neither suffering, accumulation, cessation, nor the path, one has already entered the Buddha-wisdom and is clearly enlightened.
Unimpeded wisdom has already attained the fruit of Bodhi. Although one enters the Buddha-wisdom, it is the fundamental wisdom of the original mind’s prajñā-emptiness.
Prajñā is "wisdom-less"; there is nothing it does not know. This untainted wisdom is like having no wisdom at all.
Though the fruit of Bodhi is attained, it is likewise the direct manifestation (pratyakṣa) of the original mind; the mind itself is the Buddha.
There is no need to seek it externally, nor is there anything to be attained. If one speaks of "having wisdom," this is merely a conceptual knowledge derived from a biased mind through inference;
it is not the fundamental wisdom of true emptiness and non-outflow (*anāsrava*). If one says there is something attained, there is necessarily something lost.
Since the fundamental mind of outflows is already fully endowed with fundamental wisdom, it is said that "there is neither wisdom nor attainment."

"Because there is nothing to be attained. This is a phrase that承接 (links) what precedes and initiates what follows. It means that the fundamental wisdom and fundamental dharma of the one mind are inherently complete from the beginning;

there is no dharma outside the mind that can be attained. If there were even a single dharma to be attained, it would mean that a portion of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the consciousness-mind has not yet been exhausted.
If the habitual tendencies of the consciousness-mind are exhausted, then all phenomena are fundamentally [the one mind].
Possess the single mind. The single mind inherently possesses all phenomena; the single mind and all phenomena are non-dual.
All phenomena and the fundamental mind are fundamentally one. What, then, is there to be attained?
*Bodhisattva*, *bodhisattva*. In the Sanskrit language, *bodhisattva*; in the Chinese language, *púsà* (Bodhisattva).
"By means of the *prajñāpāramitā*"—taking the *prajñāpāramitā* as the method of cultivation—one guards the six sense faculties and severs the six sensory objects;
this refers to the causal basis, meaning one relies upon the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of *prajñā*.
Fundamental wisdom. Because one awakens to it and cultivates it oneself to reach the other shore, the mind is free from hindrance.
"Hindrance" (*guà*) means being suspended and struck; "obstruction" (*ài*) means being blocked and stifled.

By relying on the fundamental wisdom of the one mind, not relying on the karmic consciousness of dependent origination, and not dwelling in the delusive dharmas of adventitious dust, then the mind is the empty mind, and dharmas...
All phenomena are empty. That is to say, by not relying on even a single dharma, the mind abides eternally;
having already attained great mastery, what further obstruction could there be?
Because there is no hindrance, the mind is free from attachment, obstruction, and impediment.
There is no fear—fear being like sinking into the earth, being blown by the wind, being burned by fire, drowning in water, or facing violent death through slaughter.
Since the five aggregates do not exist, one is eternally pure and eternally tranquil; unmoving and unshakable, all is suchness (*tathatā*). Furthermore, what [could there be]?
Is there such a thing as alarm, fear, and dread?

One must remain far removed from inverted dreams and delusions. "Inversion" refers to the confusion caused by the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), whereby false thoughts (*vikalpa*) form karma, leading to cycles of birth and extinction, and the empty, illusory turning of the wheel—these are the various inversions.
"Dreams and delusions" refers to being bewildered by the guest-dust of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
Dust is but delusive dreams and false imaginings. If there is no longer any fear, then the hindrances and defilements are exhausted;

the original nature will no longer be deluded, and false illusions will not arise again. Furthermore, what karma could there be to induce rebirth within the three realms, leading to the cycle of transmigration and inversion?
And what delusions of views and thoughts could there be to cause such delusive dreams and false imaginings?
Ultimate *nirvāṇa*. *Nir* means "non-arising"; *vāṇa* means "non-extinction. This refers to the fact that the original mind is fundamentally free from obstruction and fundamentally free from fear.
All various kinds of inverted dreams and delusions arise solely from beginningless ignorance and are nothing but false karmic consciousness.
Now, by relying on the fundamental wisdom of the single mind within this very body, one externally ceases all conditions.
The inner mind is without agitation; the mind is like a wall or a barrier. Nothing enters from without, and nothing issues forth from within.
It is true permanence, true bliss, true self, and true stillness. Ultimately, it leads directly to the Great Way of Nirvana, which is neither arising nor ceasing.
One reaches the state of neither birth nor death, and only then does one stop. This is not only the case for Bodhisattvas.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time—namely, the Buddhas of the three periods of time—who wish to attain unsurpassed enlightenment, do so by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā;
there is likewise none who does not rely on the Prajñāpāramitā.
One attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. *Anuttara* means "unsurpassed" (*an-ūrdhva*). *Samyak* means "perfectly equal" (*samyak*).
*Saṃbodhi* means "perfect awakening" (*saṃbodhi*). It is free from all dualistic opposition;
because there is nothing above it, it is called *anuttara*, meaning "unsurpassed. The original mind and original wisdom are each inherently complete. Therefore...

The term *sammyaksa* means "perfectly equal. Because the original mind’s prajñā-wisdom is fundamentally never obscured by the defilements of worldly toil, it is called *samyaksambodhi*, or "perfect enlightenment.

This refers to the fundamental mind and primordial wisdom that practices profound prajñā, reaching the further shore of the pāramitās and realizing the fruit of bodhi—not only for Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, but for all.

It is so. Indeed, all Buddhas of the three periods—past, present, and future—without exception, have attained the Great Way of Unsurpassed, Perfect, and Complete Enlightenment by relying upon the Prajñāpāramitā.
Therefore, know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is the knowledge of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
It is a great divine mantra (*mahāvidyāmantra*), a secret language of unfathomable transformation. It governs the myriad phenomena;
"divine" (*shen*) refers to its inconceivability. "Mantra" (*zhou*) refers to the secret heart-seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*).
This is the great vidyā-mantra; this is the secret word of the divine light that shines universally.
It is called "vidyā" because it illuminates all things, pervading everywhere without exception.
This is the unsurpassed mantra; this is the ultimate, peerless secret word, which is the most supreme of all and is without superior.
It may be ascended; thus it is called "unsurpassed.
It is the mantra of the unequaled. It is the secret language that is solitary, absolute, and peerless. All things are equal;
there is nothing equal to it—this is what is meant by "the equal of the equal."
It can eliminate all suffering; that is to say, it brings about deliverance from all the sufferings and calamities of birth, death, and afflictions.
It is true and not false. The Buddha speaks no lies. What the Tathāgata has spoken is true speech, real speech, suchness-speech, non-deceptive speech, and non-contradictory speech.
Therefore, I shall now proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā mantra; there is yet another secret mantra which, if recited as it is, can give rise to wisdom and enable one to reach the other shore.
Then he spoke the mantra, saying: "Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. "Gate gate" means to go forth; it is by going forth that one delivers others.
"Pāragate," repeated, means to go beyond; it is by going beyond oneself that one delivers others.
*Pāra-saṃgati*: wishing to reach the other shore; it must rely upon this wondrous truth (*saddharma*).
*Saṃgha*: the assembly. *Svāhā*: swiftness; it means the swift accomplishment of the welfare of all sentient beings.
"Bodhi svāhā. Generally speaking, all mantra-utterances are the collective secret mantras of all Buddhas.
Although they serve as paths for spiritual practice, these paths do not exist apart from this mind. If a person can empty the five aggregates, [the goal is attained].
Thus, the host remains eternally settled, while the guest-sentiments naturally clear away; how could there be anyone who fails to attain unsurpassed bodhi?
This subtle and secret heart-seal cannot be conceptualized by the conscious mind, nor should one rashly attempt to provide an interpretation of it.
Not only is it impossible to provide an annotation, it is also unnecessary to do so.

One should simply remain profoundly still and tranquil, without thought or deliberation, single-mindedly maintaining the recitation. Without marks or numbers, the mantra is the mind, and the mind is the mantra.
No longer establishing views through cognition or perception, one maintains this single-minded recitation until cognition and perception themselves are realized.
When there is no [false] view, the hosts of māras descend here; true suchness abides herein. Obstructions and terrors are liberated herein;
inverted dreams and delusions are distanced from herein. Fundamental wisdom and fundamental insight are developed herein;
ignorance and afflictions are completely extinguished herein. Thus, ignorance itself is great wisdom. It is...
Afflictions are bodhi; bodhi is the five aggregates; the five aggregates are the dharmakāya; the dharmakāya is all phenomena;
all phenomena are the mark of emptiness; the mark of emptiness is the single mind of this very body;
and this single mind of this very body is the Tathāgatagarbha. This is the Heart Mantra of the Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra.
How inconceivable are these merits!
May these merits be universally extended to all; may we and all sentient beings together believe, accept, and practice them.
Homage to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Jeta Grove Assembly (recite three times).
Vajra Mantra:
Oṃ chliṃ. Oṃ bhūliṃ. May the Buddhas manifest their bodies. Caraka spirits. Hāraka spirits. Recite the Buddha’s name one thousand times.
The ghosts depart from the body; the body leaves the bed; the illness departs from the body. All malevolent spirits and demons are transformed into dust.
There is also the *Tārā-dhāraṇī* of the Grass Deities, and there is also the *Dhāraṇī* of the Ghosts and Spirits. No evil ghosts or spirits shall be able to slander it.
We reverently invoke the Ten-Stages Vajra-Extinction. Homage to the Earth-Shaking Vajra. Homage to the Mountain-Emerging and Water-Running Vajra. Homage to...

The Vajras descend from heaven across the four seas. Homage to the Vajra of Father and Mother. If there is one who can recite the Vajra Mantra, they shall be spared from calamities surrounding their person.
The light of heaven and the light of earth, the divine radiance day and night—when this is so, spirits and Buddhas arrive of their own accord, and malevolent demons are extinguished.
If there are good men or good women who daily recite one fascicle with a tranquil mind, it is as if they have recited three hundred thousand fascicles of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Furthermore, they shall receive the protective empowerment of the divine spirits and be sustained by the various deities; their wisdom will comprehend heaven and earth.
If there are those who transcribe a copy and circulate it among others, their merit will be as lofty as Mount Sumeru and as deep as the great ocean.
O Ocean! Of immeasurable merit, may you never again tread the gates of hell for all eternity. May the Dharma be heard everywhere.
Svāhā!
